title: Game 4: Capablanca–Znosko-Borovski
subtitle: Do not reject a sound plan in search of a grand combination

narration.say: Capablanca has White at St. Petersburg in 1913. Black chooses the McCutcheon Variation of the French Defence.
White exchanges in the centre and disrupts Black’s kingside. Black damages White’s queenside in return.
White develops and advances c4. Instead of castling toward Black’s intended attack, White castles queenside.

steps.title: Gain activity with a rook lift

narration.say: Black also castles queenside. Both sides bring major pieces into action.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Attack the queen on f5 with the knight.

narration.say: White gains time with f4, drives the queen away and attacks Black’s bishop.
White advances c5. Black fixes the pawn with c6.

steps.title: A good position still needs a patient plan

narration.say: Capablanca plays Nd2, rejecting a rook manoeuvre because it seemed too slow. He criticises this decision in his notes.
Black brings the knight to b6. White checks and advances the central pawn.
White plays c4, hoping for a grand combination. Capablanca later prefers a knight manoeuvre.
Black breaks in the centre. White retreats the queen, and both sides create advanced pawns.
Black can invade the second rank with check.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Invade c2 with check.

steps.title: The advanced pawn does not guarantee victory

narration.say: Black checks with the other rook and brings the queen to e7.
White captures the pawn on d3. Capablanca believes he missed a final chance to improve here.
White manoeuvres the queen, but Black’s pieces remain active.
White moves the king to c1. Black takes the advanced pawn, then invades the first rank with check.
White resigns. We stop at the final move of the game rather than adding the mating analysis from the editorial footnote.

steps.title: Do not demand brilliance from every position

narration.say: White gained a strong position through active development and purposeful exchanges.
Capablanca then rejected patient play because he wanted a quicker, grander combination.
Black defended actively and turned the tables. A far-advanced pawn is not enough if the enemy’s pieces attack your king.
